Borrowed from French remis (“put back, reset”), the masculine singular past participle of remettre (“to put back, reset”); compare the French expression partie remise “drawn game”. Mittō is probably from Proto-Italic *meitō (“send, put forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“exchange, remove”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk remis, Danish remis, Swedish remi (“draw”) and German remis (“drawn, tied”).

1000141.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately through the widespread European name tradition represented by Portuguese Guiné (“Guinea”). The precise route by which the name entered Norwegian is uncertain. Portuguese Guiné (“Guinea”) was well established by the fifteenth century; Gomes Eanes de Zurara completed the first version of his Crónica da Guiné in 1453. Related European forms, however, are older than the Portuguese maritime expansion: Gunuia occurs on a Genoese map from around 1320 and Ginyia in the Catalan Atlas of 1375.

1004749.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse bjarmalandsferð (“journey to Bjarmaland”), from Bjarmaland (“Bjarmaland”) + ferð (“journey, expedition”). The place name Bjarmaland is formed from bjarmar (“Bjarmians”) and land (“land”); the ethnonym is probably derived from a Finnic name.
